title: A Glance at the US Housing & Rental Market
text:
Explore how economic, demographic, and housing factors influence rental versus homeownership trends across U.S. cities (2015–2023).


Introduction
Choosing to rent or buy a home is one of the most consequential financial and lifestyle decisions individuals face. In recent years, rising housing costs, shifting employment patterns, and demographic changes have reshaped the U.S. housing landscape. This project digs into the interplay of macro-level forces—such as GDP growth, mortgage interest rates, and supply constraints—with micro-level drivers like household composition, income distribution, and local population growth to understand who rents, who owns, and why.

We begin by assembling a comprehensive dataset spanning 2015 through 2023, drawing on the U.S. Census Bureau for demographic indicators, FRED (Federal Reserve Economic Data) for economic metrics, and Zillow for real-estate market statistics. After cleaning and normalizing these inputs, we engineer new features—such as home-price‐to‐income ratios and rental vacancy rates—that capture affordability and availability pressures in each metropolitan area.

Using interactive visualizations, we then explore questions like:
- How do fluctuations in mortgage rates correlate with shifts in homeownership versus rental shares?
- To what extent do changes in household types (e.g., single‐person vs. family households) explain regional rental patterns?
- Which cities buck national trends, and what local factors drive those exceptions?
By combining scatter-matrix plots, bubble‐chart comparisons, grouped boxplots, and parallel‐coordinate views, we deliver a multi-angle portrait of the housing market. Our goal is to equip policymakers, urban planners, and prospective residents with clear, data-driven insights into the forces shaping rental and homeownership across America.


Explore the Visualizations
Select an analysis below:


🔍 View 1 - Factors: Mortgage rates, GDP, Household type
A snapshot of pairwise relationships among key variables—mortgage rates, GDP, household type, and rental rates. Hover to view city-specific data points.

🔍 View 2 - Factors: CPI, Unemployment rate
Compare rental and homeownership rates across CPI and Unemployment rate. Bubble size represents population; color encodes factor categories.




🔍 View 3 - Factors: Income Tier, Education Attainment and Elderly Rate
Visualize the distribution of rental and ownership rates across factor quartiles. Identify contrasts and outliers.

🔍 View 4 - Factors: MortgageRate, GDP and Non-Single Household
Trace multivariate trends by following lines through dimensions to detect correlated movements.



🔍 View 5: Suitability choropleth



Data & Methodology

Data Sources: U.S. Census Bureau, Federal Reserve Economic Data (FRED), Zillow

Time Frame: 2015–2023

Process: Data cleaning, normalization, feature engineering, and interactive Quarto visualizations

title: View 5: Suitability choropleth
text:
Imagine you are a graduate student deciding where to move in the United States. Ideally, you seek:

Lower living costs,
Strong economic growth,
Good wage prospects.

Instead of automatically picking major cities (which often come with high salaries but also unaffordable housing), or random small towns (which may have limited economic growth and lower wages), you can now use our choropleth map to make a data-driven choice.
We created a choropleth of the United States, where each MSA is represented as a point colored from red to green based on a new feature we developed called “Suitability.”

Green: most suitable areas for personal and professional development.
Red: least suitable areas.

The Suitability score was sort based on: Housing affordability rankings, GDP (as an indicator of overall economic health), Income per capita (wage levels), Growth trends of each above from 2014 to 2023.


Code
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import geopandas as gpd
import plotly.graph_objects as go
df = pd.read_csv("../data/affordability_with_rgdp_income.csv")
df_23 = df[df["Year"] == 2023].drop(columns="Year")
df_15 = df[df["Year"] == 2015].drop(columns="Year")
df_cmp = df_23.merge(
    df_15,
    on="RegionName",
    suffixes=("_2023", "_2015")
)

for col in ["HomeownerAffordability", "RenterAffordability", "rgdp", "income_per_capita"]:
    df_cmp[f"pchange_{col.lower()}"] = (
        df_cmp[f"{col}_2023"] - df_cmp[f"{col}_2015"]) / df_cmp[f"{col}_2015"]
    
df_homeowner_sorted = df_cmp.sort_values(
    by=["HomeownerAffordability_2023","rgdp_2023","income_per_capita_2023","pchange_homeowneraffordability","pchange_rgdp","pchange_income_per_capita"],
    ascending=[ True, False,  False, True, False, False ]
)
df_homeowner_sorted = df_homeowner_sorted.reset_index(drop=True)
df_homeowner_sorted["rank"] = df_homeowner_sorted.index + 1
df_renter_sorted = df_cmp.sort_values(
    by=["RenterAffordability_2023","rgdp_2023","income_per_capita_2023","pchange_renteraffordability","pchange_rgdp","pchange_income_per_capita"],
    ascending=[ True, False,  False, True, False, False ]
)
df_renter_sorted = df_renter_sorted.reset_index(drop=True)
df_renter_sorted["rank"] = df_renter_sorted.index + 1
cbsa = gpd.read_file("../data/cb_2023_us_cbsa_20m/cb_2023_us_cbsa_20m.shp")
cbsa = cbsa.to_crs(epsg=4326)
cbsa["centroid"] = cbsa.geometry.centroid
df_centroids = pd.DataFrame({
    "geofips": cbsa["GEOID"],           
    "name":    cbsa["NAME"],            
    "latitude":  cbsa.centroid.y,
    "longitude": cbsa.centroid.x
})
df_centroids['geofips'] = df_centroids['geofips'].astype(int)
df_centroids.head()
df_homeowner_sorted = df_homeowner_sorted.merge(df_centroids, left_on = "Geofips_2015", right_on="geofips")
df_renter_sorted = df_renter_sorted.merge(df_centroids, left_on = "Geofips_2015", right_on="geofips")

import geopandas as gpd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from shapely.geometry import Point
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.patheffects as pe
import folium
import plotly.express as px
gdf_r = gpd.GeoDataFrame(
    df_renter_sorted,
    geometry=gpd.points_from_xy(
        df_renter_sorted.longitude,
        df_renter_sorted.latitude
    ),
    crs="EPSG:4326"
)

gdf_h = gpd.GeoDataFrame(
    df_homeowner_sorted,
    geometry=gpd.points_from_xy(
        df_homeowner_sorted.longitude,
        df_homeowner_sorted.latitude
    ),
    crs="EPSG:4326"
)

renter_trace = go.Scattergeo(
    lon = gdf_r.geometry.x,
    lat = gdf_r.geometry.y,
    mode = 'markers',
    marker = dict(
        size=5,
        color=gdf_r["rank"],
        colorscale="Viridis",
        cmin=gdf_r["rank"].min(),
        cmax=gdf_r["rank"].max(),
        colorbar=dict(
        tickmode="array",
        tickvals=[gdf_r['rank'].max(), gdf_r['rank'].min()],
        ticktext=["Least suitable", "Most suitable"],
        tickfont=dict(size=14),
        title=""
    )
    ),
    hovertext=gdf_r["RegionName"],
    customdata=np.stack([gdf_r[["RenterAffordability_2023","rgdp_2023","income_per_capita_2023"]]], axis=-1),
    hovertemplate="<b>%{hovertext}</b><br>Rank: %{marker.color}<br>Affordability 2023: %{customdata[0]:.2f}<br>Real GDP 2023: %{customdata[1]:.2f}<br>Income per capita 2023: %{customdata[2]:.2f}<extra></extra>",
    name="Renter Suitability",
    visible=True
)

homeowner_trace = go.Scattergeo(
    lon = gdf_h.geometry.x,
    lat = gdf_h.geometry.y,
    mode = 'markers',
    marker = dict(
        size=5,
        color=gdf_h["rank"],
        colorscale="Viridis",
        cmin=gdf_h["rank"].min(),
        cmax=gdf_h["rank"].max(),
        colorbar=dict(
        tickmode="array",
        tickvals=[gdf_h['rank'].max(), gdf_h['rank'].min()],
        ticktext=["Least suitable", "Most suitable"],
        tickfont=dict(size=14),
        title=""
    )
    ),
    hovertext=gdf_h["RegionName"],
    customdata=np.stack([gdf_h[["HomeownerAffordability_2023","rgdp_2023","income_per_capita_2023"]]], axis=-1),
    hovertemplate="<b>%{hovertext}</b><br>Rank: %{marker.color}<br>Affordability 2023: %{customdata[0]:.2f}<br>Real GDP 2023: %{customdata[1]:.2f}<br>Income per capita 2023: %{customdata[2]:.2f}<extra></extra>",
    name="Homeowner Suitability",
    visible=False
)

fig = go.Figure()
fig.add_trace(renter_trace)
fig.add_trace(homeowner_trace)

fig.update_layout(
    updatemenus=[
        dict(
            type="buttons",
            direction="right",
            x=0.5,
            y=1,
            buttons=list([
                dict(label="Renter Suitability",
                     method="update",
                     args=[{"visible": [True, False]},
                           {"title": "Renter Purchase Suitability Map (Mainland US)"}]),
                dict(label="Homeowner Suitability",
                     method="update",
                     args=[{"visible": [False, True]},
                           {"title": "Home Owner Purchase Suitability Map (Mainland US)"}]),
            ]),
            showactive=True
        )
    ]
)

fig.update_geos(projection_type="albers usa")
fig.update_layout(
    title_text="US Housing Suitability Map",
    margin=dict(l=0, r=0, t=50, b=0)
)

fig.show()

text:
Boxplots reveal both distribution and variability at a glance. In this Grouped Boxplot view, we compare rental and ownership rates across quartiles of a selected factor:

Choose Income Tier to see how low-, mid-, and high-income markets differ in tenure share.

Each box shows the median, interquartile range, and outliers—helping you answer questions like “Which income group has the widest spread of rental rates?” or “Do high-education cities show consistently higher ownership?”

title: Conclusions & Recommendations
text:
Conclusions
After exploring U.S. metro-area data from 2015 to 2023, we arrive at four main take-aways:

Home Values Drive Ownership
Metropolitan areas with higher average home values consistently show higher homeownership rates, indicating that rising property prices both reflect and reinforce local buying power.
Rent Affordability Shapes Rental Markets
Rental rate correlates most strongly with renter affordability and median income tiers. Younger adults (25–34) face the steepest rent burdens, driving up overall rental rates in those MSAs.
Education Splits the Market
Areas with a larger share of residents holding a bachelor’s degree or higher have significantly higher homeownership rates and lower rental rates compared to low-education areas.
Macroeconomic Influences Vary

Inflation (CPI): Higher CPI periods are modestly associated with increased rental activity, as buyers delay purchases.

Unemployment: Spikes in unemployment correlate with short-term dips in homeownership, though with a lag of about one year.




Recommendations

For Policymakers

Implement targeted down-payment assistance or favorable mortgage terms in high-price MSAs to bolster first-time buyers.

Expand rental vouchers and enforce rent‐stabilization measures in markets where renter affordability falls below 30% of income.

For Urban Planners

Increase supply of multifamily housing near transit and job centers, especially in high-demand age cohorts (25–34).

Incentivize mixed-income developments to avoid displacement in rapidly gentrifying neighborhoods.

For Households & First-Time Buyers

Monitor macro trends (inflation, unemployment) when locking in mortgage rates—consider fixed-rate loans during low CPI volatility.

Leverage education or income-based programs (e.g., teacher/home-buyer credits) to access lower mortgage rates.
